extmeta.ImageDescription:
An incomplete ceramic tile with hobnail impressions, dating to the Late Roman period. It is oval in shape with a light orange brown colouring. The tile is cracked and significant damage can be seen along the edges and on the back. On one side is a collection of seven circles, most likely the imprint of a hobnail boot. There is a lump of white concretion on the front, that is likely much later in date.


The tile was located clsoe to the 3rd century Roman fort of Othona at Bradwell-on-Sea, which was constructed around the time of the Carausian Revolt AD286-296. Based on this, it is assumed that the tile likely dates to the late 3rd or 4th century AD,

The tile is 2.60g weight, 103.95mm length, 77.41mm width, 23.00mm thickness

extmeta.ImageDescription:
An incomplete medieval - early post medieval glazed ceramic floor tile from the Low Counties (also known as 'Flemish' tiles) dating early 14th - 16th century. The tile is made from a red clay with a dark-green glaze on one side, which is now cracked, chipped and in parts discoloured to a bright yellow. The tile was originally square but approximately half the tile has broken off, leaving one jagged and uneven edge. The piece contains two original rounded corners, one complete original edge. On the glazed side of one corner a small hole is visable (1.1mm diameter); this hole was possibly made by a small nail used to suspend a piece of wood over the tile, used as a size template. The tiles measures (maximum) 122.1mm x 77.9mm x 27.3mm.

Similar tiles have been found in London, and have been published by Samuel & Smith (2011:268) who note that "plain-glazed tiles, imported from the Low Countries from the early 14th until the 16th century...After demoulding and before glazing, the tiles were knife-trimmed along their edges using a square wooden template as a guide. To prevent this from slipping, small nails were knocked into it and these pressed into the clay; no attempt was made to plug the tiny holes thus formed and they are a distinguishing mark of the Low Countries tiles." Similar floor tiles have also been recorded on the Portable Antiquities Scheme database e.g. LON-7B4C57; LON-963BF7; LON-DE7641.

Reference: Samuel, M and Smith, T. P. 2011. Stone and ceramic building materials. In Burch, M. Treveil, P and Keene, D. 2011. The Development of early medieval and later Poultry and Cheapside. Excavations at 1 Poultry and vicinity, City of London. Monograph 38 Museum of London Archaeology, London.

extmeta.ImageDescription:
A fragment of ceramic tile of Post-Medieval date. The fragment is irregularly shaped, sub-rectangular in section. The upper face is smooth and contains a hand-impressed retrograde image of a tree. Four deep finger impressions represent the foliage and it has three linear, projecting branches extending from the top of a trunk to the edges of the finger impressions. The trunk is represented by five diagonal lines stacked on top of each other and terminates at the base in two lines representing roots extending outwards and downwards from the trunk. The reverse of the tile has a wide, concave depression at the upper side and the whole is covered in a hard (and now cracked) resinous substance, presumably utilised in the adherence of the tile onto a flat surface. The fabric is a hard, grey-black material with abundant ill-sorted calcite and flint inclusions, both measuring 0.3-2.5mm and rare quartzite rounded pebbles measuring c.1mm

The sherd is 94.8mm long, 78.8mm wide, 27.6mm thick and weighs 195g.

Thanks are extended to Adam Parker, Collections Facilitator at the Yorkshire Museum, for his assistance in identifying this object.
